plan.topic: Plague vs COVID: one is a bacterium, one is a virus. How each spreads, who passes it on, how each is treated, and why public-health tools work differently against them
plan.angle:
Keep the plan as written, with these changes.

STATUS LINE: re-check at publish time and give each line its own date and the body that said it. As of Oct 6, 2026, WHO (spokesperson Christian Lindmeier, via UN News) said authorities are looking into whether pneumonic plague caused the death of a laboratory worker in Irkutsk oblast who died, and no official cause of death has been confirmed. Russia's Rospotrebnadzor reported 'pneumonia of unknown etiology' and said testing found no microorganisms linked to the patient's work. Use the date Rospotrebnadzor gave that statement, not the date an article was published. Russian authorities reported no dangerous pathogens among contacts, and none had symptoms. Not confirmed isn't ruled out. Put the newest development first. If you use WHO's risk assessment, quote it exactly ('moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole and very low for the WHO European region'), credited to WHO on Oct 6, 2026.

ROW 2: use CDC's wording, 'Transmission of these droplets is the only way that plague can spread between people', for pneumonic plague. Bubonic and septicemic plague come from flea bites or from handling an infected animal (CDC).

ROW 3: 'Typically, this requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague' (CDC; mention sick cats as CDC's example). Don't claim plague is 'not airborne at all'. Just contrast it with CDC's description of COVID spreading through shared air, including from people without symptoms.

ROW 4: plague 'can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early' (CDC/WHO). No drug names or doses. Say nothing about a plague vaccine. For COVID, just say that CDC lists vaccines and antiviral treatments.

ROW 5: use CDC's exact line, 'Person-to-person spread has not been documented in the United States since 1924.'

CLOSE: as planned, using CDC's 4 pneumonic signs: possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain means contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. Then 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'

Title: 'Plague vs COVID: How Each Spreads and Why They're So Different' is fine. Thumbnail: a labelled bacterium and virus, no doom words, no patient, no skulls or rats.

plan.why:
Replaces the dropped L1. It's a rising, evergreen comparison that names both sides, can be checked against stable CDC/WHO pages, and avoids the diagnostics wording and dated-statement problems that got L1 held. | fact-check: Good evergreen topic. It names both sides, sticks to agency sources and matches the 'Plague vs COVID: how each spreads' item on the playbook. The core facts check out against primary sources. Three things need fixing before scripting.

(1) The planned status line is out of date and too weak. Since the plan was written, Rospotrebnadzor has reported that the worker was diagnosed with 'pneumonia of unknown etiology'. It also said that 'based on the results of extensive testing, no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities were detected in the patient's sample' (Snopes, Oct 5, 2026). The UN News piece of Oct 6, 2026 quotes WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier: authorities 'are looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death', no official cause of death has been confirmed, all contacts were identified and monitored with none showing symptoms, and Russian authorities reported 'no pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases were detected among any of the contacts'. 'Suspected in media reports' alone leaves out what the authorities have said.

(2) Row 2 should use CDC's exact wording. CDC 'How Plague Spreads' (updated May 15, 2024) says: 'Transmission of these droplets is the only way that plague can spread between people.' It also says: 'Typically, this requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague' (sick cats are the example). CDC overview (updated Aug 24, 2026) says plague 'can be cured with antibiotics, but these must be given promptly'.

(3) For the calming US fact, CDC's exact line is 'Person-to-person spread has not been documented in the United States since 1924.' Don't mix it up with the separate 1924–1925 Los Angeles rat-associated outbreak line on the same page.

WHO's dated risk assessment, as quoted by UN News on Oct 6, 2026, is: 'moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole and very low for the WHO European region', and it will be updated as new information comes in. If the script uses it, quote it word for word with the date and speaker. Don't name or picture the worker. Media outlets name her; we don't.

package.description:
In one important way, COVID is harder to stop. It isn't about which is deadlier.
Status as of Oct 9, 2026: plague has not been confirmed in the case of a laboratory worker in Irkutsk oblast who died, and it hasn't been ruled out. Irkutsk oblast governor Igor Kobzev said monitoring of all contacts was complete.

Quick answer: COVID spreads through droplets and very small particles, even from people without symptoms (CDC). Pneumonic plague spreads between people through droplets, which CDC says typically requires direct and close contact. Plague can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early (CDC/WHO).

Possible exposure and fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

Sources:
1. CDC, How Plague Spreads: https://www.cdc.gov/plague/causes/index.html
2. CDC, About COVID-19: https://www.cdc.gov/covid/about/index.html
3. WHO, Plague fact sheet: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/plague
4. CGTN (Oct 9, 2026): https://news.cgtn.com/news/2026-10-09/Quarantine-completed-in-Russia-s-Irkutsk-after-lab-worker-s-death-1R5QbwUlFfy/p.html

script.working_title: Plague vs COVID: How Each Spreads and Why They're So Different
script.hook_pattern: Counterintuitive claim + open loop (plague sounds scarier, but COVID is harder to stop; payoff: CDC's 1924 fact and the cat in CDC guidance)

scenes.narration: Plague sounds far scarier than COVID. But in one important way, COVID is the harder one to stop. And the reason has nothing to do with how deadly each one is.

visual.stock_query: labelled bacterium and virus facing off

scenes.narration: Both can cause pneumonia. Both can pass from one person's lungs to another person. But one is a bacterium and one is a virus, and that single difference changes almost everything.

visual.stock_query: two cartoon lungs with germ labels

scenes.narration: It changes how each one spreads, who passes it on, how each is treated, and why public-health tools work so differently against them.
scenes.retention_device: Roadmap of what viewers will get

scenes.narration: Stick around to the end for a fact from CDC that goes back more than 100 years and puts US risk in perspective. And somewhere along the way, a pet cat shows up in the official guidance.

visual.stock_query: old calendar page and curious cat

scenes.retention_device: Open loop (1924 fact) plus second loop (the cat)

scenes.narration: But first, what has actually been said about the case in the news.

The newest update: on Oct 9, 2026, Irkutsk oblast governor Igor Kobzev said medical monitoring of all contacts of a laboratory worker in Irkutsk oblast who died had been completed, and that nearly 5,000 lab tests found no dangerous pathogenic microorganisms.
On Oct 7, WHO's Maria Van Kerkhove said WHO doesn't know what caused the death.
Earlier, on Oct 6, WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said authorities are looking into whether pneumonic plague caused the death, and that no official cause of death has been confirmed.

WHO also said on Oct 6 that all contacts had been identified and were being monitored, and none to date had shown symptoms. Russian health authorities reported that no pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases were detected among any of the contacts.
By Oct 6, Russian authorities had reported the diagnosis as pneumonia of undetermined origin, meaning the cause hadn't been identified.
Rospotrebnadzor said extensive testing found no evidence the illness was caused by any of the pathogens the worker handled at the institute.

On Oct 6, WHO assessed the risk as moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole, and very low for the WHO European region. WHO said it would update that as new information comes in.

visual.quote: moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole and very low for the WHO European region
visual.stock_query: map with soft colour risk zones

scenes.narration: So, as of Oct 9, 2026, plague has not been confirmed. It hasn't been ruled out either. This changes fast, so check the latest from WHO and Russian health authorities.

visual.fact: As of Oct 9, 2026: not confirmed, and not ruled out

scenes.narration: Now, why compare any of this to COVID? Because both can hit the lungs. Under a microscope, though, they're completely different kinds of germ.
Plague is caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium. WHO says it's usually found in small mammals and their fleas.
COVID-19 is caused by a virus called SARS-CoV-2.
Bacteria are living things made of a single cell. They can grow and multiply on their own.

visual.stock_query: single cell bacterium dividing in two

scenes.narration: Viruses are much smaller than bacteria. They can't reproduce on their own, so they invade living cells and use them to make copies.
Picture a bacterium as a tiny, self-contained factory. A virus is more like a set of blueprints that takes over your factory to build more of itself.
That's why the medicine cabinet looks different for each. Antibiotics are the usual treatment for bacterial infections. They don't work on viral infections, like COVID.

visual.fact: Antibiotics don't work for viral infections like COVID

scenes.narration: Treatment is where this story ends, though. Let's start where it begins: how each germ actually gets into a person.

visual.stock_query: winding path from germ to person

scenes.narration: Plague comes in three main forms, and they don't all spread the same way.
Bubonic plague affects the lymph nodes. Septicemic plague is in the bloodstream. Pneumonic plague is in the lungs.

visual.stock_query: body outline with three highlighted zones

scenes.narration: According to CDC, bubonic and septicemic plague usually come from flea bites or from handling an infected animal without proper precautions, like gloves.
But if those forms aren't treated and the bacteria spread to the lungs, CDC says the illness can become pneumonic plague.

visual.stock_query: arrow from lymph node to lungs

scenes.narration: And pneumonic is the form that can pass between people. CDC explains that someone with plague pneumonia may cough droplets containing the bacteria into the air, and another person can breathe them in.
In CDC's own words: transmission of these droplets is the only way that plague can spread between people.

visual.quote: Transmission of these droplets is the only way that plague can spread between people.

scenes.narration: But there's a catch. CDC says, typically, this requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague.

visual.quote: Typically, this requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague.

scenes.narration: Wait, animal? Here's the cat we promised. CDC says cats are particularly susceptible to plague, and sick cats can pass infectious droplets to their owners or to veterinarians.
Now compare COVID. CDC says it spreads when an infected person breathes out droplets and very small particles that contain the virus.
Other people can breathe those in, or they can land in the eyes, nose or mouth.
That's why CDC's advice for respiratory viruses like COVID includes taking steps for cleaner air where people live and work.
So here's the first big contrast. Plague's person-to-person spread typically needs direct, close contact. With COVID, the shared air itself is part of the risk.

items: Pneumonic plague: typically direct, close contact
COVID: droplets and tiny particles in shared air
visual.stock_query: split screen close contact vs room

scenes.narration: But how a germ travels is only half the story. The bigger difference is who's spreading it, and when.
scenes.retention_device: New open loop before section change

scenes.narration: During COVID, one question shaped almost everything: can people spread it before they feel sick?
For COVID, the answer was yes. CDC says people can spread COVID even if they don't have symptoms.
In 2021, a CDC modeling study of the early pandemic estimated that about 59% of COVID transmission came from people without symptoms.

visual.stat_label: Estimated early COVID spread, no symptoms

scenes.narration: In that baseline estimate, 35% came from people who hadn't developed symptoms yet, and 24% from people who never developed them at all.
Think about what that means for tracking it. You can't trace contacts from a person who doesn't know they're infectious.
The study's authors concluded that identifying and isolating people with symptoms alone would not control the ongoing spread.
Pneumonic plague looks very different. A 2005 review of pneumonic plague outbreaks found that spread typically happened through close contact with people who were already sick and coughing.
scenes.on_screen_text: Plague: spread from the visibly sick

scenes.narration: The review linked most spread to the later stage of illness, when patients were coughing.
That's what makes plague contacts findable. When someone is visibly ill and coughing, health teams can work out who was close to them.
Timing helps too. WHO says people infected with plague often develop symptoms after an incubation period of 1 to 7 days.
For COVID, CDC says symptoms may appear 2 to 14 days after exposure.
A shorter window means health authorities can watch plague contacts over a short period.

visual.stock_query: short hourglass next to long one

scenes.narration: So plague spreads at closer range and is easier to trace. But untreated, it's far more dangerous. Which brings us to the biggest difference of all.
WHO says plague can be a very severe disease. Untreated, bubonic plague has a case-fatality ratio of 30% to 60%, and the pneumonic and septicaemic forms are always fatal when left untreated.
That's what gives plague its reputation. But notice the key words: when left untreated.
Here's what changes everything. Plague can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early.
CDC is clear that antibiotics must be given promptly. And WHO says recovery rates are high for pneumonic plague if it's detected and treated in time, within 24 hours of symptoms starting.
So if you've seen claims online that plague has no cure, that's not what CDC and WHO say.

visual.fact: Plague can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early (CDC, WHO)
visual.stock_query: phone screen with crossed out claim

scenes.narration: Which antibiotic, and for how long, is a decision for doctors. That's why the right move with any concern is medical care, not treating yourself.
COVID is a virus, so antibiotics don't treat it. Instead, CDC lists vaccines and antiviral treatments.

visual.stock_query: vaccine vial and pill bottle cartoon

scenes.narration: Put them side by side. Plague: a bacterium, cured with antibiotics. COVID: a virus, with vaccines and antivirals.
And that difference in treatment unlocks something powerful for plague: a way to protect people before they ever get sick.
When pneumonic plague is suspected, health authorities have a well-tested playbook.
Isolate and treat the patient. Trace close contacts. Give contacts preventive antibiotics where health authorities decide it's needed. And watch them for symptoms.
Those preventive antibiotics are possible because plague is a bacterial infection. And they're given by health authorities, never self-prescribed.
Here's a real example. In 2017, Madagascar had a large plague outbreak in its cities, including the capital, Antananarivo.

visual.stock_query: map of Madagascar with city pins

scenes.narration: Researchers reported 2,414 suspected cases between August and November. Most were the pneumonic form, and about a quarter were confirmed or probable plague.

visual.stat_label: Suspected cases (about 1 in 4 confirmed or probable), Aug–Nov 2017

scenes.narration: Plague spreading in a crowded city sounds like the worst case. WHO reported 202 deaths. But all 7,289 contacts identified completed a course of preventive antibiotics, and by Nov 27, 2017, WHO reported no new confirmed pneumonic cases since Nov 14.

visual.stock_query: health teams visiting homes in city

scenes.narration: COVID needed a different toolbox. When a virus spreads before symptoms and through shared air, chasing contacts can't keep up on its own.

CDC's core prevention strategies for respiratory viruses include immunizations, hygiene, steps for cleaner air, and, when you're sick, staying home and away from others, and seeking care promptly for treatment if you have risk factors for severe illness.

items: When sick: stay home; seek care promptly if at higher risk

scenes.narration: Notice those are layers. They protect people even when nobody knows who's infectious.
So the tools follow the germ. With plague: find the sick, find their close contacts, and use antibiotics early. With COVID: layered protection that doesn't depend on knowing who's sick.

items: Plague: find the sick, trace contacts, antibiotics early

scenes.narration: Which brings us back to that fact we promised at the start.
Plague hasn't disappeared. WHO says that during 2019 to 2025, most cases reported to WHO occurred in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar.

visual.stock_query: world map with two highlighted countries

scenes.narration: In the United States, CDC says an average of five human plague cases are reported each year, mainly in the western US.

visual.stat_label: Average US human cases a year (CDC)

scenes.narration: And here it is. In CDC's words: person-to-person spread has not been documented in the United States since 1924.

visual.quote: Person-to-person spread has not been documented in the United States since 1924.

scenes.narration: That's more than a century with no documented spread between people in the US.
Plague and COVID can both reach the lungs. But how close you need to be, who's spreading it and when, and whether antibiotics can stop it make them very different threats.

visual.stock_query: bacterium and virus on balance scale

scenes.narration: Here's your quick checklist.
One: plague is a bacterium, COVID is a virus. Two: pneumonic plague spreads between people through droplets, typically with direct and close contact.

items: Pneumonic plague: droplets, typically direct and close contact

scenes.narration: Three: plague can be cured with antibiotics, especially when started early. Four: COVID can spread without symptoms, so CDC's tools include vaccines, cleaner air and antivirals.

items: Plague: cured with antibiotics, especially when started early
COVID: can spread without symptoms; vaccines, cleaner air, antivirals

scenes.narration: If you live in or visit an area where plague occurs, CDC's prevention steps include reducing rodent habitat around your home and keeping fleas off your pets.
With flea products, follow the label. Some dog flea products, such as permethrin, are toxic to cats.

visual.stock_query: cat and dog with product label

scenes.narration: And the most important part. If you've had a possible exposure, like close contact with someone with pneumonic plague or a sick animal, and you develop fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently.
scenes.on_screen_text: Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently

scenes.narration: Tell them about the possible exposure so they can act fast. And remember: as of Oct 9, 2026, plague had not been confirmed in the Irkutsk oblast case, and the Irkutsk oblast governor said monitoring of all contacts was complete. Check the latest official updates.
If you're worried, talk to a health professional.
Next, we're explaining how long health authorities watch plague contacts, and why. Subscribe so you get the answer, minus the panic.

factcheck.summary:
The science holds up. I checked the plague and COVID numbers, quotes and study descriptions against the source pages, and they are accurate: the CDC quotes in s26, s27 and s69 are word for word. The safety lines are all there: flea-product label caveat, the 4 CDC pneumonic signs, "contact a doctor or local health authority urgently", "If you're worried, talk to a health professional" and no self-treatment.

One major problem needs fixing before publish. The news section skips the Oct 8 development: WHO Director-General Tedros asked Russia about media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause, and Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that "the vast majority of what the media is reporting regarding this situation is false information" (Al Jazeera, Oct 8; CBC also reports a denial by Russian health officials). Without it, the "as of Oct 9" summary is incomplete and leans more reassuring than the record supports.

There are also some minor fixes: the "not ruled out" line should say who holds that view, and a few source dates and titles are wrong. The ITV/AP page timed out when I tried to open it. Search results confirm it exists with that title on Oct 7, and copies of the same AP story say what s06b and s10 claim.

I searched for news from Oct 9–10 and found no change to the official status after the governor's Oct 9 update.

issues.location: s06b–s07 (news section; new scene needed between s06b and s07)
issues.claim: The status summary runs Oct 9 → Oct 7 → Oct 6 and skips Oct 8.
issues.problem: It leaves out a material, dated development. On Oct 8, WHO Director-General Tedros urged Russia to respond to 'media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause'. The same day, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that 'the vast majority of what the media is reporting regarding this situation is false information' (Al Jazeera, Oct 8; CBC reports a denial by Russian health officials). A status decoder that leaves out a reported second illness, and the dispute over it, is incomplete, and the reassuring 'monitoring complete' framing could mislead.
issues.fix: Add scene s06c after s06b. Narration: "On Oct 8, WHO's Director-General said WHO was seeking information from Russia about media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause. The same day, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said most of what the media was reporting about the situation was false information. Those reports have not been confirmed." On-screen text: "Oct 8: second-case reports NOT CONFIRMED". Source: add {id: "aljazeera-2026-10-08", title: "Russia dismisses reports of second plague case, WHO urges formal response", publisher: "Al Jazeera", year: "2026", url: "https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/8/russia-dismisses-reports-of-second-plague-case-as-false-information"}.

issues.claim: "So, as of Oct 9, 2026, plague has not been confirmed. It hasn't been ruled out either."
issues.problem: 'Not ruled out' is said in our own voice with no source. Russian authorities say testing found no link to the pathogens she handled and report pneumonia of undetermined origin, while WHO says it doesn't know the cause. The line should be credited to the body that actually said it.
issues.fix: Narration: "So, as of Oct 9, 2026, plague has not been confirmed. Russian authorities report pneumonia of undetermined origin, and WHO said on Oct 7 it doesn't know the cause, so it hasn't been ruled out either. This changes fast, so check the latest from WHO and Russian health authorities." Keep the on-screen text "NOT CONFIRMED, NOT RULED OUT" together on one caption screen.

issues.claim: "as of Oct 9, 2026, plague had not been confirmed in the Irkutsk oblast case, and the Irkutsk oblast governor said monitoring of all contacts was complete."
issues.problem: This leaves out the unconfirmed Oct 8 second-case reports, which makes the recap more reassuring than the record.
issues.fix: Narration: "And remember: as of Oct 9, 2026, plague had not been confirmed in the Irkutsk oblast case, the Irkutsk oblast governor said monitoring of all contacts was complete, and Oct 8 reports of a second ill employee had not been confirmed. Check the latest official updates."

issues.problem: The CDC 'Symptoms of COVID-19' page is dated March 10, 2025.
The PetMD page is dated April 8, 2025.
issues.fix: Year: "2025"; title: "Is It Safe to Use Dog Flea Products on Cats? (updated Apr 8, 2025)".

issues.problem: The page's published title is 'Signs and Symptoms of Plague'.
issues.fix: Title: "Signs and Symptoms of Plague (updated May 15, 2024)".

issues.claim: "...or from handling an infected animal without proper precautions, like gloves."
issues.problem: CDC's wording is 'handling tissue or body fluids of a plague-infected animal'. Its gloves example is a precaution for hunters. The script's phrasing narrows the source and makes it sound like blame.
issues.fix: Narration: "According to CDC, bubonic and septicemic plague usually come from flea bites or from handling tissue or body fluids of an infected animal. CDC advises precautions like gloves."

issues.claim: "The review linked most spread to the later stage of illness, when patients were coughing."
issues.problem: Kool's wording is 'endstage', when patients 'cough copious amounts of bloody sputum', and transmission happens 'only by means of close contact'. 'Later stage' softens it. That's acceptable, but it's more accurate to use the source's own term.
issues.fix: Narration: "The review found people usually spread it only in the end stage of illness, when they were coughing heavily, and only through close contact." On-screen text: "End stage, heavy coughing".

thumbnail.reasoning: Candidate #1 ("1924" big-number) best fits both general thumbnail best practice and InforMed's own data: specific, credible numbers have been our strongest-performing plague hook (e.g., the CDC US-case number thumbnail got the best YouTube/Instagram results), and a single bold number plus a sleepy bacterium icon gives one unmistakable focal point that's instantly legible at phone size. It's calm and factual (no doom framing), matches the dated/credited-fact guardrail, and creates a clean curiosity gap ("why does a 1924 date answer which disease is harder to stop?") that the video can pay off. Candidate #0 has good contrast and curiosity but the red-X/green-check iconography risks looking like a value judgment on the diseases themselves rather than illustrating difficulty-to-stop, which is a legibility-of-meaning issue even though the text is readable. Candidate #2 only shows the COVID icon with no plague counterpart, so it doesn't actually represent the 'vs' promise of the title and reads as one-sided. All three clear the 7+ legibility bar, so CTR and clarity of concept decide it: #1 wins.

issues.problem: The checked script quotes CDC: person-to-person spread 'has not been documented in the United States since 1924'. Saying it was the 'last' spread is slightly stronger than CDC's wording, because CDC only says no later spread has been documented.
